moduleMetadata.title: Women's Digital Safety & Online Privacy
moduleMetadata.description: Empowering women and girls to navigate digital spaces with confidence through privacy control, identity protection, and informed response strategies.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Women's digital safety is essential for ensuring confident, secure participation in digital life. By understanding how to protect personal information, secure accounts, and respond effectively to threats like harassment or online blackmail, users can maintain control over their digital identities and privacy.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users will be able to recognize common digital risks, implement robust privacy controls, and apply a structured response model when facing online safety incidents.

learningObjectives: Define women's digital safety and its core goals: Protect, Control, Respond.
Identify common digital risks including harassment, impersonation, and blackmail.
Implement privacy controls on social media and personal accounts.
Apply the WHO/WHAT/WHERE/WHEN/WHY framework to evaluate posting risks.
Preserve evidence correctly in the event of an online safety incident.
Recognize the signs of account takeover and fake support scams.
Utilize a structured response framework (S.A.F.E.R.) for managing blackmail and AI-manipulated content.
Navigate Pakistan-specific reporting and support resources.

sections.title: Module Purpose
sections.content: This module is designed to help women and girls protect themselves from common digital threats such as:
sections.callout:
The objective is not to discourage women from using technology.

MilcharSec helps users use digital platforms confidently while maintaining control over their privacy, identity, accounts, and personal information.

sections.title: 1. What Is Women's Digital Safety?
sections.content:
Women's digital safety means protecting yourself from risks that can occur through:

Social media
Messaging applications
Email
Online communities
Cloud accounts
Smartphones
Laptops
Educational platforms
Shopping platforms
Professional networks

subsections.title: Protect
subsections.content: Protect your accounts, devices, and information.

subsections.title: Control
subsections.content: Control who can access or see your information.

subsections.title: Respond
subsections.content: Know what to do when something goes wrong.

sections.title: 2. Common Digital Risks
sections.content: MilcharSec should introduce users to the following risks.

rows: Someone gains access to your social account
Someone creates a fake account using your identity
Someone learns where you regularly go
Someone uses private information to pressure you
Someone pretends to be another person
Fake messages designed to steal information
Personal information is obtained without authorization

sections.callout: Experiencing an online safety problem is not the victim's fault.

sections.title: 3. Protect Your Main Email Account
sections.content:
Your primary email account deserves special protection because it can often be used for account recovery.

MilcharSec recommends:
bulletPoints: Do not reuse the password on other websites.

quiz.question: Which account should receive particularly strong protection?
options: A. An account you never use

sections.title: 4. Social-Media Privacy
sections.content: Users should regularly review:
checklist: Profile visibility — Who can see your profile?
Posts — Who can see your posts?
Stories — Who can view temporary content?
Messages — Who can send you messages?
Tags — Who can tag or mention you?
Searchability — Can strangers find you using your email or phone number?

sections.title: 5. Privacy Setting Simulator
sections.content:
For your deployed MilcharSec platform, make this interactive.

Show a fictional social-media profile:

Profile: Sarah

Then give switches:
sections.callout:
Privacy Exposure: HIGH

Reasons:
Phone number publicly visible
Location enabled
Unknown users can message
Everyone can tag the account

Then allow the user to click: Improve My Privacy

The platform explains each setting.

sections.title: 6. Location Privacy
sections.content:
Location information can reveal patterns.

For example:

Home → University → Gym → Home

Repeated location sharing can potentially reveal someone's routine.

Safer Practices
Users should consider:
Reviewing location permissions.
Avoiding unnecessary real-time location sharing.
Checking which apps have location access.
Reviewing location-related social-media settings.
Considering whether a location needs to be posted publicly.
sections.callout:
Location services themselves are not necessarily dangerous.

Give location access only when it is necessary and appropriate.

sections.title: 7. Think Before Posting
sections.content: Before posting something publicly, ask:
framework: Does it reveal where I am right now?
Does everyone who can see it actually need this information?

sections.title: 8. Photo Privacy
sections.content:
Photos may contain more information than the user realizes.

Check for:
sections.callout:
Photo Privacy Checklist

User uploads or selects a sample image.

Possible personal information visible in the image.

For the first deployment, I recommend making this a privacy checklist rather than automatic facial/person identification.

sections.title: 9. Fake Profiles & Impersonation
sections.content:
Someone may create an account pretending to be you.

Possible indicators:
Your name
Your photograph
Similar username
Your biography
Your university/work information
Messages sent pretending to be you
steps: Record the profile URL if available.
Report the account to the platform.
Report serious cases to the appropriate authority.

sections.title: 10. Interactive Tool — Fake Profile Detector
sections.content:
Users can enter information about a suspicious profile.

Input: Profile name; Username; Account age; Profile picture; Messages received; Claims made by account.

Educational analysis can identify indicators such as:
sections.callout:
Low Concern
Needs Verification
High Concern

This is an educational assessment. It cannot confirm whether an account is genuine or malicious.

sections.title: 11–14. Unwanted Contact, Cyberstalking, Online Harassment, Threats & Blackmail
sections.content:
Examples: Repeated DMs; Unwanted friend requests; Persistent comments; Repeated calls; Messages from multiple accounts.

Cyberstalking can involve repeated unwanted online behavior directed toward a person. Examples may include: Repeated unwanted communication; Persistent monitoring; Multiple fake accounts; Repeated unwanted contact after being asked to stop; Attempts to obtain private information.

You don't have to respond to someone simply because they contact you.

Harassment may include: Abusive messages; Repeated unwanted contact; Threatening messages; Fake accounts; Coordinated abuse; Unwanted public posts.

Don't engage unnecessarily. Instead: Preserve → Block/Restrict → Report → Seek Support.

If someone uses private information to threaten or pressure you:
do: Seek appropriate professional/legal help when necessary

sections.title: 15–16. Evidence Preservation and Evidence Checklist
sections.content: This should be an important interactive section in MilcharSec. Teach users to preserve:
sections.callout: Don't manipulate or edit evidence unnecessarily.

sections.title: 17–19. Account Takeover, MFA Protection and Fake Support Accounts
sections.content: Possible warning signs:
sections.callout:
Secure → Verify → Report → Recover

MFA provides an additional layer of account security. Never approve an MFA request you did not initiate. If unexpected MFA requests repeatedly appear: Do not approve them. Preserve the information. Review account security. Report the activity when appropriate.

An attacker may pretend to be: Instagram Support; Facebook Security; Account Recovery Team; Cybersecurity Department. They may ask for: Password; OTP; MFA code; Recovery code; Personal information.

Never give your password or authentication code to someone who contacts you unexpectedly claiming to be support.

sections.title: 20–24. Digital Identity, University, Recovery, Device Safety and Personal Digital Safety Score
sections.content:
Avoid unnecessarily publishing: CNIC information; Phone number; Home address; Personal email; Daily routine; Travel plans; University schedule; Workplace schedule; Private family information. This does not mean users must hide their identity. It means: Share information intentionally.

A student posts: Every Monday and Wednesday I am in Lab 4 from 9 AM–1 PM. What information has been exposed? Routine; University location; Time pattern; Regular schedule. Avoid unnecessarily publishing detailed routines publicly.

Account Recovery Safety: Use the official account recovery process; Verify the correct website/app; Change compromised passwords; Enable MFA; Review active sessions; Review recovery email/phone; Report unauthorized access. Never give recovery codes to strangers claiming to help.

Device Safety Checklist: Screen lock; Automatic locking; Updated operating system; Updated applications; App permissions reviewed; Unknown applications removed; Account sessions reviewed.

Personal Digital Safety Score questions: Is MFA enabled on your main email? Do you reuse passwords? Is your phone number publicly visible? Is your profile public? Do you share your real-time location publicly? Can strangers message you? Do you review app permissions? Do you have a screen lock? Do you know how to report harassment on platforms you use? Do you know where to report cybercrime in Pakistan?

Result: Digital Safety Score: 78/100. Strong Areas: Account protection; Device security. Improve: Location privacy; Social-media visibility. Recommended Actions: Review location settings; Restrict profile visibility; Enable MFA on remaining important accounts.

sections.title: 25–30. Pakistan — Get Help & Report
sections.content:
National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency — NCCIA

The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) is Pakistan's current dedicated cybercrime investigation agency. Its official site provides cybercrime reporting information and specifically includes cyber-harassment guidance.

Report Cybercrime: NCCIA Official Website: https://www.nccia.gov.pk/
Online Complaint Portal: https://complaint.nccia.gov.pk/
Helpline: 1799

NCCIA's FAQ says complaints can also be initiated through the Pakistan Citizen Portal and that formal investigation is handled through NCCIA's Cybercrime Reporting Centres.

NCCIA — Cyber Harassment: NCCIA specifically advises users not to overshare personal information, to secure social-media accounts, use safer browsing practices, and avoid unnecessary interaction with unknown people. It lists 1799, its complaint system, and an official email as reporting channels. https://www.nccia.gov.pk/harrasment.php

Digital Rights Foundation — Cyber Harassment Helpline: Helpline 0800-39393; Email helpdesk@digitalrightsfoundation.pk. DRF describes the service as free and confidential and says it assists people facing online harassment and digital-security threats. Label this Support / Guidance rather than presenting it as a law-enforcement reporting agency.

Pakistan Citizen Portal: https://web.citizenportal.gov.pk/

Cybercrime / Online Abuse: Fake account; Online harassment; Account compromise; Cyberstalking; Online blackmail; Unauthorized sharing. Use the appropriate cybercrime reporting/support channel.

Immediate Physical Danger: If a user believes they face an immediate physical safety emergency, MilcharSec should tell them to contact appropriate local emergency services or a trusted person immediately rather than relying only on an online complaint.

sections.title: 31–34. Help UI, Privacy Design and Educational Risk Assessment
sections.content:
Need Help? Report Cybercrime — NCCIA — Helpline: 1799 — https://complaint.nccia.gov.pk/
Cyber Harassment Support — Digital Rights Foundation — 0800-39393 — https://digitalrightsfoundation.pk/
Government Complaint Portal — Pakistan Citizen Portal — https://web.citizenportal.gov.pk/

Interactive I Need Help options: My account was hacked; Someone is harassing me; Someone created a fake profile; Someone is threatening/blackmailing me; My private information was shared; Someone is repeatedly contacting me; My device/account may be compromised; I don't know what happened. Then MilcharSec gives: Immediate Safety Steps; Evidence Checklist; Account Protection Steps; Platform Reporting Guidance; Pakistan Reporting Resources.

Do NOT permanently store sensitive incident information unless there is a clear reason and proper consent. For interactive tools, preferably: Process → Analyze → Display Result → Delete Input. Your input is processed for this assessment and is not permanently stored. Only make this statement if your actual implementation truly does this.

Do not ask users for unnecessary information: Passwords; OTP/MFA codes; Recovery codes; CNIC numbers for educational checks; Private photos unnecessarily; Exact home address; Unnecessary personal information. Collect the minimum information required to provide the feature.

Every automated result should include: Educational Assessment Only. This assessment does not establish that a crime has occurred. If you believe you are at risk, preserve relevant information and consider contacting an appropriate support or reporting service.

sections.title: 35–38. Final Scenario, Quiz, Checklist and Module Completion
sections.content:
Scenario: A student discovers a fake Instagram account using her name and photograph. The account is contacting people pretending to be her.

Step 1: Preserve relevant evidence.
Step 2: Secure her own account.
Step 3: Avoid unnecessary engagement with the impersonating account.
Step 4: Report the fake account through the platform.
Step 5: Seek support if needed.
Step 6: If the situation constitutes cybercrime or serious harassment, consider reporting it to NCCIA.

Correct Response: PRESERVE → SECURE → REPORT → SEEK SUPPORT

Final Knowledge Quiz
Q1. Should you share your MFA code with someone claiming to be support? No.
Q2. Should real-time location always be publicly shared? No.
Q3. What should you do if someone creates a fake profile using your identity? Preserve evidence, report the profile, secure your account, and seek appropriate help.
Q4. What should you do with serious online threats? Preserve relevant information, seek support, and report appropriately.
Q5. What is the current Pakistani cybercrime agency? NCCIA — National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency.
Q6. What is the NCCIA cybercrime helpline? 1799.
Q7. What organization provides a Cyber Harassment Helpline? Digital Rights Foundation.
Q8. What is its listed helpline? 0800-39393.

MilcharSec Women's Digital Safety Checklist
Accounts: Unique passwords; MFA enabled; Recovery options secured; Unknown sessions removed.
Device: Screen lock; Automatic locking; Updated OS; App permissions reviewed.
Social Media: Profile privacy reviewed; Unknown messages restricted; Tags controlled; Phone/email visibility reviewed.
Location: Location permissions reviewed; Real-time sharing limited; Routine not unnecessarily public.
Photos: Background checked; IDs/documents hidden; Location considered; Audience checked.
Online Abuse: Evidence preserved; Account reported; Trusted person informed; Appropriate authority contacted if necessary.

Remember: PROTECT → CONTROL → THINK → PRESERVE → REPORT
Your digital identity belongs to you. You have the right to use technology without surrendering unnecessary control over your privacy.

Pakistan Resources: NCCIA — Cybercrime Reporting: https://complaint.nccia.gov.pk/; NCCIA — Official Website: https://www.nccia.gov.pk/; Digital Rights Foundation — Digital Safety Support: https://digitalrightsfoundation.pk/; Pakistan Citizen Portal: https://web.citizenportal.gov.pk/

MilcharSec Core Habit: YOUR DATA. YOUR ACCOUNT. YOUR PRIVACY. YOUR CONTROL.

sections.title: Session 2 — Online Blackmail, Deepfakes & AI-Manipulated Videos
sections.content:
This session teaches users how to respond safely when someone: Threatens them using private information; Claims to possess private images/videos; Uses manipulated images or videos to impersonate them; Creates AI-generated or AI-manipulated content involving them; Threatens to publish or distribute fake content; Demands money or other actions; Creates fake social-media profiles using their identity.

If someone threatens you with fake or manipulated content, you are not responsible for what the attacker created.

Digital blackmail is when someone uses digital information, images, videos, messages, or claims to pressure or threaten another person. The content may be genuine, manipulated, completely fabricated, or AI-generated. A threat does not prove that the person actually has what they claim.

AI tools can manipulate a person's face, voice, photograph, video, audio, background, or text. The result can appear convincing even when it is not genuine. These technologies are often referred to as deepfakes or synthetic/manipulated media.

AI-manipulated content can potentially be used for impersonation, harassment, fraud, reputation attacks, extortion, misinformation, and privacy violations. A video looking realistic does not automatically mean it is authentic.

Example: A student receives a message: I created a video of you. Send me money or I will publish it. The student does not know whether the video is real or manipulated. Don't panic. Don't send money. Don't send additional personal information. Don't forward the content to other people. Instead: Preserve relevant evidence; Stop unnecessary communication; Secure affected accounts; Report the account/content; Tell a trusted person; Seek appropriate professional or legal support if necessary.

sections.title: Session 2 — S.A.F.E.R., What NOT To Do and Evidence
sections.content: The BLACKMAIL Response Model — S.A.F.E.R.
framework: Don't continue unnecessary negotiation with the person.
Preserve relevant messages, account information, URLs, and timestamps.
Change compromised passwords, enable MFA, and review account sessions.
Report the account/content and use appropriate support or law-enforcement channels.
dont: Don't send money simply because they demand it.
Don't forward the suspected content unnecessarily.
Don't publicly post the suspected content to prove it is fake.
sections.callout:
Create an Incident Evidence Checklist rather than asking users to upload intimate or highly sensitive content to your platform. Your platform should not encourage victims to upload intimate images/videos for AI analysis. Instead, your UI can ask: Do you have evidence of the incident? Screenshot → Save securely → Record account details → Report.

There is no single visual clue that proves a video is fake. Possible warning signs can include: Strange facial movements; Inconsistent lighting; Unnatural lip synchronization; Audio that doesn't match the person; Unusual transitions; Inconsistent background details; Unnatural speech patterns; Visual inconsistencies; Contradictory context. These signs are not definitive proof.

Context Verification: Who originally posted it? Where did it first appear? Is there an original source? Does the surrounding context make sense? Is the person actually known to have been present? Are multiple trustworthy sources reporting the same event? Has the supposed person or organization confirmed it?

sections.title: Session 2 — Verification Exercise and Blackmail + Fake AI Content Scenario
sections.content:
AI Video Verification Exercise: A video appears online showing a person saying something they supposedly never said. A. Immediately assume it is real. B. Immediately assume it is fake. C. Investigate the source and context and avoid spreading it until verified. D. Download and repost it. Correct Answer: C.

Blackmail + Fake AI Content Scenario
Situation: Someone contacts a woman through social media. They claim: I have an embarrassing video of you. They demand money. They send a suspicious video that appears to show her.

Step 1 — STOP
Don't immediately respond to the demand.

Step 2 — DON'T PAY OR PROVIDE INFORMATION
Don't provide additional information or authentication codes.

Step 3 — PRESERVE
Record relevant account and message information.

Step 4 — SECURE
Review account security and enable MFA.

Step 5 — REPORT
Report the account and content to the platform.

Step 6 — SEEK SUPPORT
Tell a trusted person and consider appropriate professional/legal support.

sections.title: Session 2 — Tools, Reporting, Emergency Screen and Decision Tree
sections.content:
AI Media Awareness Checker — not 100% Deepfake Detector, because automated systems cannot guarantee that a piece of media is real or fake. Accept a publicly available or non-sensitive sample media file for educational demonstration. It can explain: Possible visual inconsistencies; Audio/video synchronization issues; Contextual concerns; Source information if available; Why automated analysis is uncertain. Results: No obvious indicators detected; Potential manipulation indicators; Multiple manipulation indicators. Disclaimer: This tool provides an educational assessment and cannot guarantee that media is authentic or manipulated. Do not rely on an automated result for legal or safety decisions.

Blackmail Response Assistant options: Someone is threatening me; Someone created a fake profile; Someone claims to have private content; Someone shared manipulated content; Someone is demanding money; Someone is repeatedly contacting me; Other. If selected: Someone is threatening me with a fake video. First: Don't panic. Protect: Secure your important accounts. Preserve: Save relevant evidence. Don't: Don't send passwords, OTPs, or additional private information. Report: Report the account/content through the platform. Get Support: Contact a trusted person and appropriate support/reporting services.

Pakistan — Reporting Cyber Harassment & Blackmail: NCCIA Helpline: 1799; NCCIA Official Website: https://www.nccia.gov.pk/; NCCIA Online Complaint Portal: https://complaint.nccia.gov.pk/; NCCIA Cyber Harassment Information: https://www.nccia.gov.pk/harrasment.php; Digital Rights Foundation Cyber Harassment Helpline: 0800-39393; Pakistan Citizen Portal: https://web.citizenportal.gov.pk/

I'm Being Blackmailed: You don't have to handle this alone. Do now: Secure your accounts; Preserve relevant evidence; Don't share passwords or OTPs; Avoid unnecessary communication; Report the account/content; Tell someone you trust; Use appropriate reporting/support channels.

Interactive Decision Tree: Are you being threatened? YES. Is the person demanding money or another action? YES. Is the content possibly fake/manipulated? YES / DON'T KNOW. Don't try to prove it yourself. Preserve relevant evidence. Secure accounts. Report the account/content. Seek support. Pakistan: NCCIA — 1799; DRF — 0800-39393.

sections.title: Session 2 — Knowledge Quiz, Remember Card and Recommended Placement
sections.content:
Q1. Does a realistic-looking AI video automatically prove that it is genuine? No.
Q2. Should you give someone your password because they threaten you? No.
Q3. What should you preserve? Relevant evidence such as messages, account details, timestamps, and URLs.
Q4. Should victims upload intimate content to MilcharSec for analysis? No.
Q5. What should you do before sharing suspicious AI-generated content? Verify the source and context.
Q6. What is the NCCIA cybercrime helpline? 1799.
Q7. What is the DRF Cyber Harassment Helpline? 0800-39393.

THREATENED ONLINE?
DON'T PANIC
Secure your accounts
Preserve evidence
Don't share passwords/OTPs
Don't automatically comply with demands
Report the account/content
Tell someone you trust
Contact appropriate support/reporting services

FAKE OR REAL — YOU DON'T HAVE TO HANDLE DIGITAL BLACKMAIL ALONE.

Recommended placement: Session 1 — Women's Digital Safety & Privacy → Accounts, social media, location, privacy, impersonation. Session 2 — Online Blackmail & AI-Manipulated Media → Blackmail, deepfakes, threats, evidence, response. Session 3 — Reporting & Getting Help in Pakistan → NCCIA, DRF, platform reporting, incident documentation. Interactive Tools: Digital Privacy Checker; Fake Profile Awareness Checker; Blackmail Response Assistant; AI Media Awareness Checker; Pakistan Cyber Help Directory.

keyTakeaways: Digital safety is about taking control, not avoiding technology.
Primary email accounts require the strongest possible protection (unique password + MFA).
Never pay blackmail demands; preserve evidence and seek help instead.
Automated 'deepfake detectors' for intimate content are not reliable; rely on personal discretion and support services.
Pakistan-specific resources like NCCIA (1799) and Digital Rights Foundation (0800-39393) provide necessary support.
YOUR DATA. YOUR ACCOUNT. YOUR PRIVACY. YOUR CONTROL.
reflectApply: Review your current social media privacy settings. Are there any that could be stricter?
Identify a trusted person you could contact if you experienced an online safety incident.
